claim: Chat-EGFP mice show EGFP expression in cholinergic areas including MHb, habenular projections to the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDTg), third cranial nerve (3N), basal forebrain (BF), and nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS).
source: Chat-EGFP mice show EGFP expression in cholinergic areas including MHb, habenular projections to the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), the laterodorsal tegmentum (LDTg), third cranial nerve (3N), basal forebrain (BF), and nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1A showing EGFP expression patterns in Chat-EGFP mice and the text description of these patterns.

claim: Kiaa1107-Cre mice show Cre-recombinase expression in the MHb and axonal projections in the IPN.
source: Kiaa1107-Cre mice show Cre-recombinase expression in the MHb and axonal projections in the IPN.
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1A showing Cre expression patterns and the text description.

claim: 99% (1912 of 1933) of CHAT positive neurons in the MHb are positive for the EYFP reporter in Kiaa1107-Cre mice crossed to reporter Gt(ROSA)26Sortm1(EYFP)Cos mice.
source: Double immunostaining with CHAT and EYFP antibodies in Kiaa1107-Cre mice crossed to reporter Gt(ROSA)26Sortm1(EYFP)Cos mice (Figure 1D) demonstrated that 99% (1912 of 1933) of CHAT positive neurons in the MHb are positive for the EYFP reporter.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from double immunostaining experiments.

claim: CHAT populations in striatum, PPTg and LDTg show extremely low expression of the EYFP reporter (0.5 to 1.3% of CHAT cells) in Kiaa1107-Cre mice crossed to reporter mice.
source: In contrast, CHAT populations in striatum, PPTg and LDTg show extremely low expression of the EYFP reporter (0.5 to 1.3% of CHAT cells) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The Kiaa1107-Cre line specifically targets the cholinergic population of habenular neurons without affecting other cholinergic neurons.
source: These results establish that the Kiaa1107-Cre line specifically targets the cholinergic population of habenular neurons without affecting other cholinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on the data showing high specificity in MHb (99%) and low expression in other cholinergic areas (0.5-1.3%).

claim: CHAT immunoreactivity is absent in the MHb, fasciculus retroflexus (fr) and IPN in ChAT-cKO mice.
source: Immunohistochemical analyses of brain sections clearly showed that CHAT immunoreactivity was absent in the MHb, fasciculus retroflexus (fr) and IPN in ChAT-cKO mice (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Only 0.3% habenular neurons in ChAT-cKO mice retained their immunoreactivity to CHAT.
source: This analysis showed that only 0.3% habenular neurons in ChAT-cKO mice retained their immunoreactivity to CHAT, while the number of CHAT positive neurons in striatum, PPTg and LDTg were comparable in wt and ChAT-cKO mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CHAT immunoreactivity shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The Kiaa1107-Cre strain drives Cre-recombination of the Chat conditional allele in 99.7% of habenular cholinergic neurons.
source: These data show that the Kiaa1107-Cre strain drives Cre-recombination of the Chat conditional allele in 99.7% of habenular cholinergic neurons, and that it can be used to specifically delete Chat only from habenular neurons without perturbing other cholinergic sources in the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on the quantification showing only 0.3% of habenular neurons retained CHAT immunoreactivity.

claim: The onset of Chat Cre-mediated excision by Kiaa1107-Cre occurs between postnatal days P6 and P7.
source: To determine whether Chat excision occurred during the early stages of habenular development (Quina et al., 2009), we analyzed the expression of CHAT in wt and ChAT-cKO at early postnatal ages and detected the onset of Chat Cre-mediated excision by Kiaa1107-Cre between postnatal days P6 and P7 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental analysis shown in Figure 3 and cited reference.

claim: VGLUT1 and CHAT show the strongest index of colocalization in the IPC (M1=0.80 in wt, M1=0.79 in ChAT-cKO) and no colocalization in the IPL (M1=0.005 in wt, M1=0.01 in ChAT-cKO).
source: These analyses indicated an extremely high colocalization of VGLUT1 and VACHT in the IPC of both wt (M1=0.80) and ChAT-CKO (M1=0.79), less overlap in the IPI (wt, M1=0.78, ChAT-CKO, M1=0.77) and IPR (wt, M1=0.68, ChAT-CKO, M1=0.69), and no colocalization in the IPL (wt, M1=0.005, ChAT-CKO, M1=0.01) (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Manders' colocalization coefficient analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The vast majority of cholinergic+glutamatergic input to the IPC originates in the ventral MHb.
source: Taken together with the published literature, our data demonstrate that the vast majority of cholinergic+glutamatergic input to the IPC originates in the ventral MHb.
evidence: The claim is based on colocalization data and integration with published literature.

claim: VACHT and VGLUT1 antibodies have comparable penetration and labeling immunoreactivities, including the number of labeled vesicles per synaptic terminal.
source: Quantification analyses showed that both antibodies have comparable penetration and labeling immunoreactivities, including the number of VACHT and VGLUT1-labeled vesicles per synaptic terminal (Figure 5D), the labeling density (Figure 5E) and the percentage of vesicles labeled within a terminal (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: VACHT and VGLUT1-labeled vesicles located farther than 350 nm from the active zone are differentially distributed.
source: However the scatter plot distribution showed that VACHT and VGLUT1-labeled vesicles located farther than 350 nm from the active zone were differentially distributed (F(1,936) = 4.954; p<0.05; one-way ANOVA) (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of distance measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Both VACHT and VGLUT1 transporters are present in the vast majority (80%) of habenular terminals in the central IPN.
source: We observed colabeling of VACHT-6 nm and VGLUT1-12 nm gold particles in 72 of 90 labeled synaptic terminals, 8 terminals with only VAChT-6 nm particles and 10 terminals with only VGLUT1-12 nm particles indicating that both transporters are present in the vast majority (80%) of habenular terminals in the central IPN (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by double post-embedding immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 54.35% of VGLUT1-gold particles (n=75/138) could be located in the same SV as VACHT based on a maximal distance criterion of 90 nm.
source: Considering this maximal theoretical distance of 90 nm, 54.35% of VGLUT1-gold particles (n=75/138) could be located in the same SV as VACHT (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by distance measurements between gold particles in electron microscopy images.

claim: ACh and glutamate vesicular transporters are coexpressed in 80% of the axonal terminals in the IPC.
source: These ultrastructural analyses indicate that ACh and glutamate vesicular transporters are coexpressed in 80% of the axonal terminals in the IPC, and that within each presynaptic terminal a significant fraction of SVs colabel with VACHT and VGLUT immunogold particles, supporting the conclusion that ACh and glutamate can be cotransported into the same synaptic vesicles in habenular cholinergic presynaptic terminals
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative electron microscopy data showing colocalization.

claim: Nicotine-evoked eEPSCs did not differ between wt and ChAT-cKO in MHb neurons (wt: 2265.3 ± 210.4 pA, n=18; cKO: 2467 ± 175.2 pA, n=18; p=0.465).
source: As expected, eEPSCs did not differ between wt and ChAT-cKO (wt: 2265.3 ± 210.4 pA, n=18; cKO: 2467 ± 175.2 pA, n=18; p=0.465) (Figure 7B,C), since conditional deletion of Chat in the MHb would not directly affect expression of any cholinergic genes in the stria medullaris, which gives rise to the presynaptic cholinergic input to the MHb (Contestabile and Fonnum, 1983; Gottesfeld and Jacobowitz, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and cited references explaining the mechanism.

claim: Pressure application of nicotine (100 µM) evoked medium size inward currents from IPN neurons that had similar amplitudes in wt and ChAT-cKO mice (wt: 254.3 ± 45.55 pA, n=52; cKO: 304.8 ± 51.03 pA, n=53; p=0.475).
source: Pressure application of nicotine (100 µM) evoked medium size inward currents from IPN neurons that had similar amplitudes in wt and ChAT-cKO mice IPN: wt: 254.3 ± 45.55 pA, n=52; cKO: 304.8 ± 51.03 pA, n=53; p=0.475) (Figure 7D,E), demonstrating that elimination of ACh in habenular neurons does not affect nicotine-evoked responses of postsynaptic nAChRs in MHb and IPN neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 7D-E.

claim: The average amplitude of mEPSC in IPC neurons of wt mice is 18.2 ± 1.6 pA, whereas the average amplitude in ChAT-cKO neurons is 12.4 ± 0.9 pA (p=0.005).
source: This analysis revealed that the average amplitude of mEPSC in IPC neurons of wt mice is 18.2 ± 1.6 pA; whereas the average amplitude in ChAT-cKO neurons is 12.4 ± 0.9 pA (p=0.005; wt: n=25; ChAT-cKO: n=24) (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7J.

claim: There is a 32% reduction in the amplitudes of glutamatergic mEPSC in ChAT-cKO animals compared to wt.
source: This corresponds to a 32% reduction in the amplitudes of glutamatergic mEPSC in ChAT-cKO animals, which might reflect a decrease of the vesicular content of glutamate or differences in the number or function of postsynaptic glutamate receptors (Liu et al., 1999; Watt et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the mEPSC amplitude data and cited references for interpretation.

claim: Quantitative analyses of the frequency of mEPSC showed no differences between IPC neurons of wt (5.3 ± 1.2 Hz) and ChAT-cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8 Hz).
source: Quantitative analyses of the frequency of mEPSC showed no differences between IPC neurons of wt (5.3 ± 1.2 Hz for wt) and ChAT-cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8 Hz) (Figure 7K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Superfusion with nicotine or ACh did not change the amplitudes of mEPSCs in either wt or ChAT-cKO.
source: Superfusion with nicotine (Figure 8B) or ACh (Figure 8C) did not change the amplitudes of mEPSCs in either wt, or increased the amplitudes of ChAT-cKO to wt levels, consistent with the hypothesis that the decrease of glutamate vesicular content in presynaptic terminals depends on the presence of intracellular ACh.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 8B-C and mechanistic interpretation.

claim: A significant increase in mEPSC frequency was observed in wt, but not in ChAT-cKO mice upon superfusion with nicotine.
source: Importanlty, we observed a significant increase in mEPSC frequency in wt, but not in ChAT-cKO mice upon superfusion with nicotine (Figure 8D) and ACh (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 8D-E.

claim: In the absence of network activity eliminated by TTX, nicotine or ACh activation of nAChRs at presynaptic terminals elicits enhanced discharge of glutamatergic mEPSCs in IPC neurons of wt mice.
source: This indicates that in the absence of network activity eliminated by TTX, nicotine or ACh activation of nAChRs at presynaptic terminals elicits enhanced discharge of glutamatergic mEPSCs in IPC neurons of wt mice.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the electrophysiological data showing increased mEPSC frequency upon nicotine/ACh application in wt.

claim: There is no presynaptic facilitation in ChAT-cKO neurons, suggesting that presynaptic nAChRs are downregulated in the absence of ACh released by habenular terminals.
source: In contrast there is no presynaptic facilitation in ChAT-cKO neurons, suggesting that presynaptic nAChRs are downregulated in the absence of ACh released by habenular terminals.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of mEPSC frequency increase in ChAT-cKO and mechanistic speculation.

claim: Holding currents are very similar between genotypes and upon perfusion with nAChR agonists, indicating that postsynaptic nAChRs in IPN neurons are not affected by elimination of endogenous ACh.
source: We next analyzed holding currents as a measure of the excitability of postsynaptic IPN neurons. The values are very similar between genotypes and upon perfusion with nAChR agonists (Figure 8F), indicating that postsynaptic nAChRs in IPN neurons are not affected by elimination of endogenous ACh.
evidence: The claim is supported by holding current measurements shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Western blot analyses of nAChRs and GluR1 in IPN extracts did not show significant differences between wt and ChAT-cKO.
source: Western blot analyses of nAChRs and GluR1 in IPN extracts did not show significant differences between wt and ChAT-cKO (Figure 8G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 8G-H.

claim: mEPSC amplitudes and frequencies in IPL neurons were not significantly different between wt and ChAT-cKO.
source: Cumulative and average amplitude of glutamatergic mEPSC recordings in IPL neurons identified by biocytin and SP immunostaings (Figure 9B,C) showed that mEPSC amplitudes and frequencies were not significantly different between wt and ChAT-cKO (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings in the IPL shown in Figures 9D-E.

claim: In wt mice mEPSC were smaller in the IPL with respect to the IPC and similar to the amplitudes detected in the IPC of ChAT-cKO mice.
source: It is interesting to note that in wt mice mEPSC were smaller in the IPL with respect to the IPC and similar to the amplitudes detected in the IPC of ChAT-cKO mice (Figure 7J and 9D).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of mEPSC amplitudes across different IPN regions and genotypes.

claim: Western blot analyses of isolated SVs revealed no differences in the protein levels of Synaptophysin (Syp), VACHT, VGLUT1, and VGLUT2 between wt and ChAT-cKO mice.
source: Western blot analyses of isolated SVs revealed no differences in the protein levels of Synaptophysin (Syp), VACHT, VGLUT1, and VGLUT2 between wt and ChAT-cKO mice (Figure 10A: lanes 1 and 6 and Figure 10B) indicating that loss of CHAT did not alter the expression of synaptic vesicle proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 10A-B.

claim: VGLUT1-isolated SVs were positive for VACHT and VACHT-isolated SVs were positive for VGLUT1 in both wt and ChAT-cKO vesicles.
source: Immunoisolations of SVs from wt and ChAT-cKO mice using polyclonal antibodies directed against Syp, VGLUT1, VGLUT2, and VACHT (Figure 10A) and immunoisolations with IgG antibodies as background control revealed that VGLUT1-isolated SVs were positive for VACHT and that VACHT-isolated SVs were positive for VGLUT1 (yellow squares, Figure 10A). In all cases, the immune-detected signals were comparable in wt and ChAT-cKO vesicles.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoisolation experiments shown in Figure 10A.

claim: A portion of VGLUT2-specific immunoisolates showed coexistence of VACHT in wt and ChAT-cKO vesicles.
source: Additionally, a portion of VGLUT2-specific immunoisolates showed coexistence of VACHT in wt and ChAT-cKO vesicles (blue squares Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoisolation experiments shown in Figure 10A.

claim: In the presence of 10 mM ACh iodide, vesicles accumulated significantly more [3H]glutamate compared to control condition.
source: In the presence of 10 mM ACh iodide (10 mM K-iodide was used for osmotic compensation in control condition), vesicles accumulated significantly more [3H]glutamate (mean ± S.E.M. of 12 control and 10 ACh samples from 4 experiments; unpaired t-test: *p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by glutamate uptake assay data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Addition of ACh increased vesicular glutamate uptake by 35.8 ± 13.6% relative to control vesicles.
source: Thus, addition of ACh increased vesicular glutamate uptake by 35.8 ± 13.6% relative to control vesicles.
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of glutamate uptake experiments.

claim: ACh synergizes vesicular filling of glutamate, providing functional evidence for the coexistence of VACHT and glutamate vesicular transporters in a subset of IPN vesicles.
source: Altogether, our results show that ACh synergizes vesicular filling of glutamate, providing additional functional evidence for the coexistence of VACHT and glutamate vesicular transporters in a subset of IPN vesicles.
evidence: The claim is based on the glutamate uptake data and integration with other experimental findings.

claim: Baseline activity of ChAT-cKO mice was comparable to wt.
source: Baseline activity of ChAT-cKO mice was comparable to wt (Figure 11A, B); however nicotine-induced hypolocomotion was significantly less pronounced in ChAT-cKO than in wt mice (Figure 11C), indicating that ChAT-cKO mice show reduced sensitivity to nicotine.
evidence: The claim is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figures 11A-B.

claim: Nicotine-induced hypolocomotion was significantly less pronounced in ChAT-cKO than in wt mice, indicating that ChAT-cKO mice show reduced sensitivity to nicotine.
source: Baseline activity of ChAT-cKO mice was comparable to wt (Figure 11A, B); however nicotine-induced hypolocomotion was significantly less pronounced in ChAT-cKO than in wt mice (Figure 11C), indicating that ChAT-cKO mice show reduced sensitivity to nicotine.
evidence: The claim is supported by locomotor activity measurements shown in Figure 11C and interpretation.

claim: Wt mice but not ChAT-cKO became progressively less responsive to daily injections of nicotine and locomotor depression was significantly attenuated after 5 days compared to the first day of administration.
source: Wt mice but not ChAT-cKO became progressively less responsive to daily injections of the drug and locomotor depression was significantly attenuated after 5 days compared to the first day of administration (Figure 11D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tolerance behavior measurements shown in Figure 11D.

claim: ChAT-cKO mice do not develop tolerance induced by repetitive administration of nicotine.
source: These data show that ChAT-cKO mice do not develop tolerance induced by repetitive administration of nicotine.
evidence: The claim is based on the tolerance behavior data showing no progressive decrease in response in ChAT-cKO.

claim: Wt mice treated with nicotine exhibited significantly more somatic and affective signs of withdrawal compared to wt mice drinking saccharin alone.
source: Wt mice treated with nicotine exhibited significantly more somatic (Figure 11E) and affective (Figure 11F) signs of withdrawal compared to wt mice drinking saccharin alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by withdrawal behavior measurements shown in Figures 11E-F.

claim: ChAT-cKO mice did not display altered signs of withdrawal in the treated versus untreated group.
source: In contrast, ChAT-cKO mice did not display altered signs of withdrawal in the treated versus untreated group (Figure 11E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by withdrawal behavior measurements shown in Figures 11E-F.

claim: Local elimination of ACh release by MHb neurons to IPN neurons prevents the development of nicotine withdrawal behaviors.
source: These results demonstrate that local elimination of ACh release by MHb neurons to IPN neurons prevents the development of nicotine withdrawal behaviors.
evidence: The claim is based on the withdrawal behavior data in ChAT-cKO mice.

claim: Robust preference for the nicotine-paired environment was seen in wt mice after three conditioning sessions with 1.5 mg/kg nicotine compared to the saline-paired environment.
source: Robust preference for the nicotine-paired environment was seen in wt mice after three conditioning sessions with 1.5 mg/kg nicotine compared to the saline-paired environment (Figure 11G).
evidence: The claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 11G.

claim: ChAT-cKO mice did not display CPP at any nicotine concentration tested, demonstrating insensitivity to nicotine-mediated place preference.
source: In contrast, ChAT-cKO mice did not display CPP at any nicotine concentration tested (Figure 11H), demonstrating insensitivity to nicotine-mediated place preference in ChAT-cKO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by conditioned place preference data shown in Figure 11H.

claim: Nicotine-dependent behaviors such as nicotine-conditioned reward and withdrawal are controlled by the release of ACh from MHb neurons.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that nicotine-dependent behaviors such as nicotine-conditioned reward and withdrawal are controlled by the release of ACh from MHb neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on the behavioral data showing lack of reward and withdrawal in ChAT-cKO mice.

claim: ACh production at MHb-IPN synapses is essential for the establishment of nicotine dependence.
source: The studies presented here reveal that ACh production at MHb-IPN synapses is essential for the establishment of nicotine dependence, and that local ACh action plays an important role in withdrawal responses.
evidence: The claim is based on the behavioral data from ChAT-cKO mice showing lack of nicotine dependence behaviors.

claim: Loss of ACh selectively in habenular neurons results in a reduction in the content of glutamate in synaptic vesicles isolated from the IPN.
source: We demonstrate that loss of ACh selectively in habenular neurons results in a reduction in the content of glutamate in synaptic vesicles isolated from the IPN, supporting the recent finding that MHb neurons corelease ACh and glutamate (Ren et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by the mEPSC amplitude data and cited reference.

claim: ACh has a dual role in the IPN: first, the facilitation of vesicular glutamate uptake into SVs; and second, the modulation of transmitter release through activation of presynaptic nAChRs.
source: We provide functional evidence for a dual role of ACh in the IPN: first, the facilitation of vesicular glutamate uptake into SVs; and second, the modulation of transmitter release through activation of presynaptic nAChRs.
evidence: The claim is based on the glutamate uptake data and electrophysiological findings showing presynaptic facilitation.

claim: Infusion of glutamate receptor antagonists into the IPN results in decreased nicotine intake and withdrawal.
source: Furthermore, infusion of glutamate receptor antagonists into the IPN results in decreased nicotine intake (Fowler et al., 2011) and withdrawal (Zhao-Shea et al., 2013) suggesting that glutamate-mediated fast synaptic transmission is also important in nicotine addiction.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as risk factors for nicotine dependence and lung cancer in genes encoding nAChR subunits (CHRNB3-CHRNA6 and CHRNB4-CHRNA3-CHRNA5 clusters), and in nicotine-metabolizing enzymes (CYP2A6 and CYP2B6).
source: Genome-wide association studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as risk factors for nicotine dependence and lung cancer in genes encoding nAChR subunits (CHRNB3-CHRNA6 and CHRNB4-CHRNA3-CHRNA5 clusters), and in nicotine-metabolizing enzymes (CYP2A6 and CYP2B6) (Bierut et al., 2007; Kumasaka et al., 2012; Saccone et al., 2009; Thorgeirsson et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references to genome-wide association studies.

claim: Variations in the CHAT gene have been associated with prospective smoking cessation.
source: In addition, variations in the CHAT gene have been associated with prospective smoking cessation (Heitjan et al., 2008; Ray et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Nicotine does not trigger nicotine-dependent behaviors unless the endogenous neurotransmitter ACh is released from MHb neurons to further promote glutamate corelease.
source: The studies presented here show that nicotine does not trigger nicotine-dependent behaviors unless the endogenous neurotransmitter ACh is released from MHb neurons to further promote glutamate corelease.
evidence: The claim is based on the behavioral and electrophysiological data from ChAT-cKO mice.

claim: ACh was first described in the heart muscle.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh) was first described in the heart muscle (Loewi, 1921), and later in the peripheral nervous system, as a fast acting neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction (Bennett, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited historical reference.

claim: In the central nervous system (CNS), evidence supports the hypothesis that ACh acts by volume transmission and that slowly changing levels of extracellular ACh mediate arousal states contributing to attention, sleep, learning and memory.
source: In the central nervous system (CNS), however, evidence supports the hypothesis that ACh acts by volume transmission and that slowly changing levels of extracellular ACh mediate arousal states contributing to attention, sleep, learning and memory (Dani and Bertrand, 2007; Everitt and Robbins, 1997; Mesulam et al., 1983; Picciotto et al., 2012; Ren et al., 2011; Sarter et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Cholinergic projection neurons in the medial habenula (MHb) synapse in the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), which contains extremely high levels of AChE.
source: Cholinergic projection neurons in the medial habenula (MHb) synapse in the interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), which contains extremely high levels of AChE (Flumerfelt and Contestabile, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: At synapses with a high concentration of AChE, ACh is so quickly degraded that a single molecule cannot activate a second receptor.
source: At synapses with a high concentration of AChE, ACh is so quickly degraded that a single molecule cannot activate a second receptor (Kuffler and Yoshikami, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited reference.

claim: Both nicotinic (nAChRs) and muscarinic (mAChRs) acetylcholine receptors are often localized extrasynaptically on dendrites and somata, and presynaptically at axonal terminals.
source: Since both nicotinic (nAChRs) and muscarinic (mAChRs) acetylcholine receptors are often localized extrasynaptically on dendrites and somata, and presynaptically at axonal terminals (De-Miguel and Fuxe, 2012; Descarries et al., 1997; Role and Berg, 1996), it is thought that ACh volume transmission in the IPN requires high frequency stimulation of habenular neurons (Ren et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: The release of ACh from habenular terminals is consistent with genetic studies demonstrating altered responses to nicotine addiction as a consequence of mutations in nicotinic receptors that are enriched in the MHb-IPN.
source: The release of ACh from habenular terminals is consistent with genetic studies demonstrating altered responses to nicotine addiction as a consequence of mutations in nicotinic receptors that are enriched in the MHb-IPN (Antolin-Fontes et al., 2015; Fowler et al., 2011; Jackson et al., 2010; Salas et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references.

claim: Neurotransmitters can be coreleased in several systems.
source: For example, it has been demonstrated in several systems that neurotransmitters can be coreleased (El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Gras et al., 2008; Guzman et al., 2011; Hnasko et al., 2010; Hnasko and Edwards, 2012; Ren et al., 2011; Shabel et al., 2014), and that cooperation between vesicular neurotransmitter transporters located in the same synaptic vesicle (SV) can reciprocally increase the packaging of their respective neurotransmitters into SVs, a process termed vesicular synergy (El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Gras et al., 2008; Hnasko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Cooperation between vesicular neurotransmitter transporters located in the same synaptic vesicle (SV) can reciprocally increase the packaging of their respective neurotransmitters into SVs, a process termed vesicular synergy.
source: For example, it has been demonstrated in several systems that neurotransmitters can be coreleased (El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Gras et al., 2008; Guzman et al., 2011; Hnasko et al., 2010; Hnasko and Edwards, 2012; Ren et al., 2011; Shabel et al., 2014), and that cooperation between vesicular neurotransmitter transporters located in the same synaptic vesicle (SV) can reciprocally increase the packaging of their respective neurotransmitters into SVs, a process termed vesicular synergy (El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Gras et al., 2008; Hnasko et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references defining vesicular synergy.
